DFT and Circular Convolution (L06, first half)

Why this matters in the exam: L06 (the DFT) has never been examined in a test, so it is a likely target for the final. Tutorial 5 is the only practice set, and its questions are short calculations: compute a small DFT, do a circular convolution, use the DFT for linear convolution. With an open-book paper and short multi-part questions, expect a 4-point DFT or circular convolution worth roughly 3–6 marks, often chained (DFT → multiply → IDFT → compare with linear convolution). Every calculation here is small enough to do by hand in a few minutes if you know the method.

1. The core ideas

1.1 Frequency sampling of the DTFT and time aliasing

The DTFT is continuous in . Sample it at equally spaced points, , . L06 shows that these samples are the exact spectrum of the periodic extension

  • What it means: sampling in frequency makes the time signal periodic with period . Copies of are placed every samples and added.
  • When to use it: any question that says “the DTFT is sampled at points; what sequence does the IDFT return?”
  • Trap: if length of , the copies overlap. This is time aliasing. One period of is then with its tail wrapped round and added to the start. You can only recover from the samples if (L06 slide 6: “no aliasing … N larger than the length of x(n)”).

1.4 FFT complexity

Direct DFT: outputs, each an -term sum, so about complex multiplications. Radix-2 FFT ( a power of 2): about complex multiplications (and additions). L06 quotes the order .
256 65 536 1 024 2 048
1024 1 048 576 5 120 10 240

L06 uses : vs , “100-fold reduction”. Using the multiplication count , the saving is about 205-fold. Trap: state which count you are using.

1.5 DFT vs DFS

The -point DFT is the exact line spectrum of the periodic with period (L06 slide 15):

So DFT and DFS coefficients are the same numbers up to a factor . Trap: forgetting the factor when a question gives Fourier series coefficients.

4. Traps that cost marks

  • Using in the forward DFT, or forgetting and the sign flip in the IDFT.
  • Reversing a sequence as instead of the circular reversal . This breaks both the time-reversal property and the circulant matrix.
  • Computing linear convolution when circular was asked (or the reverse). A circular answer always has exactly samples.
  • Choosing or for linear convolution via DFT. The condition is .
  • Saying zero padding “improves resolution” in the sense of separating close frequencies. It only samples more densely (true resolution is for pack D6).
  • Forgetting when converting between DFT and DFS.
  • Circular shift: using for a delay. A delay of multiplies by .
  • Deconvolution: dividing by without comment.

7. Add to your open-book reference sheet

DFT (L06)
X(k) = sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x(n) W_N^{kn},   x(n) = (1/N) sum_k X(k) W_N^{-kn},  W_N = e^{-j2pi/N}
W_4 = [1 1 1 1; 1 -j -1 j; 1 -1 1 -1; 1 j -1 -j];   W_N^{-1} = (1/N) W_N^*
Checks: X(0)=sum x(n);  x(0)=(1/N) sum X(k);  real x => X(N-k)=X*(k)
Freq sampling: N samples of X(w) <-> x_p(n)=sum_m x(n-mN). Aliasing iff N < L.
   One period: write x in rows of N, add columns.
X(k) = X(w) at w=2pi k/N  (if L <= N).   DFT vs DFS: X(k) = N c_k
FFT: direct N^2 mults; radix-2 (N/2)log2 N mults (O(N log2 N))
Properties (mod N):  x((n-l)) <-> X(k)e^{-j2pi kl/N};  x((-n)) <-> X((-k)) = X(N-k)
   x(n)e^{j2pi ln/N} <-> X((k-l));  x* <-> X*((-k));  x1 (*)N x2 <-> X1 X2
   x1 x2 <-> (1/N) X1 (*)N X2;  Parseval: sum|x|^2 = (1/N) sum|X|^2
Circular reversal of {x0,x1,x2,x3} = {x0,x3,x2,x1}
Circular conv: y(n)=sum_m x1(m) x2((n-m))_N. Circulant: col 0 = x2, shift down + wrap.
   Shortcut: linear conv, then fold samples n>=N back by N and add.
Linear conv via DFT: zero-pad to N >= L+M-1, Y=XH, IDFT.
   If N too small: first L+M-1-N samples are corrupted.
Deconvolution: X(k)=Y(k)/H(k) - fails where H(k)=0.
Check any convolution: sum y = (sum x1)(sum x2).
